newsitem.title: USA: Most urban riots not racially motivated, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Most urban riots not racially motivated, study finds.

text.p: Race has been the motivation in fewer than half the urban riots in the United States over the last two years, according to a study released on Wednesday.

Six of 21 riots in 1994 and 1995 resulted from fans being disappointed because a rock concert was cancelled or sold out or because their sporting team lost an important game, the study released by Northeastern University said.

"When Americans think of riots they think of race," said Jack Levin, a criminology and sociology professor at Northeastern University in Boston, who co-wrote the study. "But actually more than half have nothing to do with race."

In Miami in March 1994 around 2,000 rock music fans rioted after tickets to a Pearl Jam concert were sold out in 11 minutes. Five people were injured, including three police officers, and four people were arrested, the study said.

Disappointed music fans also rioted after a Grateful Dead concert was dropped in Orlando, Florida in April, 1994 and after police cancelled a Green Day concert in Boston in September, 1994. In July, 1994 15 fans were arrested for rowdy behaviour in Huntington Park, California, after Mexico's soccer team lost to Bulgaria. And Ohio State University students, upset after their football team lost a big game, set fires and pelted firefighters with bottles in Columbus in October, 1995.

But Levin said a substantial number of riots are racially motived. He found nine of the 21 riots over the past two years were sparked by racial divisions. About five of those cases were sparked by confrontations between a white police officer and a black suspect, as happened in St. Petersburg, Florida, in October and earlier this month.

"The problem is the police simply don't have credibility with black Americans in general. The police are kind of seen as an army of occupation, as representatives of a white power structure that has oppressed black Americans," Levin said.

Levin and a graduate student, Benjamin Steiner, who co-wrote the study, found the number of riots increased from nine in 1994 to 12 in 1995, a 33 percent increase which may indicate a trend. "I think at the very least this should be a warning sign of things to come," Levin said.

More disturbing, he said, was that 13 of the 21 riots involved teenagers and young adults. Demographic studies indicate that the number of teenagers is expected to increase by 17 percent over the next nine years, he said.
